concept_html:
Example tests check the cases you thought of. Property-based tests check a rule against hundreds of generated inputs, including ones you did not think of. Hypothesis generates the inputs, and when a test fails it shrinks the input to the smallest failing case. Examples use Hypothesis 6.168.

from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

@given(st.lists(st.tuples(st.floats(-1e6, 1e6), st.floats(0, 10)), min_size=1))
def test_weighted_mean_within_range(pairs):
    values = [v for v, _ in pairs]
    weights = [w for _, w in pairs]
    m = weighted_mean(values, weights)
    assert m is None or min(values) - 1e-6 <= m <= max(values) + 1e-6

Run against a weighted_mean without a zero guard, this test failed in this course's build with ZeroDivisionError, and Hypothesis shrank the input to pairs=[(0.0, 0.0)]: one value, one zero weight.

Properties that suit data code:

  • Bounds. A mean lies between the minimum and maximum. A share lies in [0, 1].
  • Invariance. Shuffling rows does not change a total. Renaming a category does not change counts.
  • Round trip. Writing then reading a file gives back the same frame.
  • Idempotence. Deduplicating twice equals deduplicating once.
  • Grain. The output has exactly one row per key.
  • Agreement. A fast implementation equals a slow, obviously correct one.

Choose strategies deliberately. st.floats() generates nan and infinities by default. Bound it (st.floats(-1e6, 1e6)) or pass allow_nan=False unless your function must handle them, and then test that behaviour on purpose. hypothesis.extra.pandas builds DataFrames with data_frames and column.

Use @settings(max_examples=...) to trade speed for coverage. Hypothesis saves failing examples in a local .hypothesis/ directory and replays them first on the next run. Add it to .gitignore.

Hypothesis does not run in this app's browser runtime. The exercises check your code's structure.

lines: from hypothesis import given, strategies as st
counts = st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=10_000)
@given(counts, counts)
def test_share_in_unit_interval(a: int, b: int) -> None:
part, total = min(a, b), max(a, b)
result = share(part, total)
assert result is not None and 0.0 <= result <= 1.0

solution_lines: from hypothesis import given, strategies as st
@given(st.lists(st.tuples(st.sampled_from(["a", "b", "c"]), st.integers(0, 5))))
def test_dedupe_idempotent(rows: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> None:
assert dedupe(dedupe(rows)) == dedupe(rows)
exercises.starter:
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st


def test_dedupe_idempotent():
    rows = [("a", 1), ("a", 1)]
    assert dedupe(rows) == [("a", 1)]

title: Property-based tests with Hypothesis
why_html: A deduplication step kept the latest record per respondent. Its example tests used three tidy rows. In production, two records for one respondent had the same timestamp, and the function kept both, so the respondent was counted twice. A Hypothesis test of the grain, "the output has exactly one row per respondent", fails on this bug at once. In this course's build it shrank the failure to rows=[('a', 0), ('a', 0)]: two identical rows.
